question:
Trying to loop through a str array and convert elements to integers

I am working on a simple problem where I sort exactly three integers in ascending order. Here's what I have written: import stdio import sys nums = sys.argv idxLow = min(nums).index idxHigh = max(nums).index numMid = 0 for i in nums: i = int(float(i)) if i != idxLow and i != idxHigh: numMid = int(float(nums[i])) stdio.write(nums[idxLow] + " " + numMid + " " + nums[idxHigh]) I keep getting ValueErrors, and no matter where I cast, the elements of the nums array, despite being integers, still return errors. Input: python three_sort.py 9 2 4 Restrictions: can only use the stdio and sys libraries, can only use min(), max(), and basic arithmetic
reference_answer: The reason you are getting the ValueError is with what sys.argv returns sys.argv actually returns the file name as the first element, and then the attributes. If you ran python three_sort.py 9 2 4 , sys.argv actually returns this: ["three_sort.py", "9", "2", "4"] now, when you loop through this list, I in the first iteration is actually "three_sort.py", and since "three_sort.py" is not possible to convert to an integer, your code fails. Here is the working code: import sys import stdio nums = sys.argv nums = [int(num) for num in nums[1:]] # Exclude the filename low = min(nums) # The index is not needed high = max(nums) numMid = 0 for i in nums: # Don't convert i if i != low and i != high: # convert i instead of nums[i] numMid = i stdio.write(f"{low} {numMid} {high}") # use f-string so we dont have to convert all integers to a string there were a few other errors: I is not an index, it is the value itself, so num[I ] won't work. You were comparing I with a string. As pointed out in the comments, for strings, "10" is less than "9", so we convert everything to integers Not only that, there is no point of using indexes, they just complicate the code Not only those things, without excluding the filename and using max() or min() , there is a chance that the filename gets selected for one of them (actually it is guaranteed).
llm_attempt:
The ValueError comes from the for-loop: sys.argv includes the script name as element 0 ('three_sort.py'), and float('three_sort.py') raises ValueError. You must skip argv[0] and use argv[1:] for the actual numbers. Separately, min(nums).index and max(nums).index are bound methods (never called, no argument), so idxLow/idxHigh are method objects, not integers - comparing an int to a method is always unequal, so that logic can't work anyway. You don't need indices at all: once you have the three ints, low=min, high=max, and mid = sum - low - high (valid with only min/max/arithmetic). Example:

nums = [int(x) for x in sys.argv[1:]]
a, b, c = nums
low, high = min(nums), max(nums)
mid = a + b + c - low - high
stdio.writeln(str(low) + ' ' + str(mid) + ' ' + str(high))

This avoids sorting, indices, and the argv[0] pitfall entirely.

question:
Pandas pd.read_csv() using single quote as quotechar throws SyntaxError: incomplete input

I am currently trying to read in a .csv with the following structure: samplecsv = """ 'column A', 'column b', 'column c', 'valueA', 'valueb', 'valuec,d', 'valueA', 'valueb', 'valuecd', 'valueA', 'valueb', 'valuecd', 'valueA', 'valueb', 'valuec,d' """ Note that I don't include it as a string but I stored the data in the same structure in a .txt file. I want python to ignore the comma in 'valuec,d' for the separation, for this value to be stored in a single column later. I found out that you can provide a to then be ignored quotechar as argument, yet I can’t get it to run with single quote. I have tried: import pandas as pd DF = pd.read_csv(r'Myfilepath', sep = ',', quotechar =''') As well as: DF = pd.read_csv(r'Myfilepath', sep = ',', quotechar ='''') I also tried: DF = pd.read_csv(r'Myfilepath', sep = ',', quotechar ="'") All 3 versions gave me SyntaxError: incomplete input . What am I doing wrong?
reference_answer: I don't get any errors with this data. The fields contain extra whitespace though, which requires the skipinitialspace parameter. The following code: import pandas as pd samplecsv = """ 'column A', 'column b', 'column c', 'valueA', 'valueb', 'valuec,d', 'valueA', 'valueb', 'valuecd', 'valueA', 'valueb', 'valuecd', 'valueA', 'valueb', 'valuec,d' """ from io import StringIO df=pd.read_csv(StringIO(csv), sep = ',', quotechar ="'",skipinitialspace=True) df Produces column A column b column c Unnamed: 3 0 valueA valueb valuec,d NaN 1 valueA valueb valuecd NaN 2 valueA valueb valuecd NaN 3 valueA valueb valuec,d NaN The final empty column is sue to the trailing , in most lines. It can be removed with dropna : >>> df.dropna(axis=1,how='all') column A column b column c 0 valueA valueb valuec,d 1 valueA valueb valuecd 2 valueA valueb valuecd 3 valueA valueb valuec,d
llm_attempt:
This SyntaxError is from Python's parser, not pandas. In quotechar=''') and quotechar='''') , three or four consecutive apostrophes get parsed as the start of a triple-quoted string ('''...), which is never closed - Python keeps waiting for the closing ''' and reports 'incomplete input' (and can swallow following lines/cells too, which is likely why even your third, valid attempt appeared to fail if run after a broken one in the same cell). Your third form, quotechar with a double-quoted string containing one single quote, is the correct syntax - run it on its own:

df = pd.read_csv(path, sep=',', quotechar="'")

Given your sample has a space after each comma before the opening quote, also add skipinitialspace=True so pandas recognizes the quote character immediately:

df = pd.read_csv(path, sep=',', quotechar="'", skipinitialspace=True)

That should keep 'valuec,d' as one field.

reference_answer: If you are using AWS API Gateway, then its default timeout is 29 seconds and might cause the issue. Time timeout can be increased. See this Amazon post for more details.
llm_attempt: A 502 from EB usually means the upstream (gunicorn) worker died or dropped the connection, not necessarily a proxy timeout - since add_task returns the HTTP response immediately, before running generate_pdf_task, so this specific request shouldn't be blocked for 30s. Two likely causes beyond nginx/gunicorn config: (1) EB's Load Balancer (ALB/CLB) has its own idle timeout, separate from nginx and your Procfile, configurable under Configuration -> Load Balancer -> Idle timeout (default 60s) - raise that too; (2) the background task itself (PDF/zip generation) spikes memory or throws an unhandled exception on the smaller EB instance, crashing the worker process; with few gunicorn workers, the next request routed to that dead worker gets a 502. Check `eb logs` / /var/log/web.stdout.log around the failure time for OOM-killer messages or tracebacks. Consider wrapping the task body in try/except with logging, increasing instance size or worker count, or offloading PDF generation to a queue (SQS/Celery) instead of an in-process BackgroundTask.

question:
Change behavior of function depending on type

I have a function where one of the variables is either a function x(t) or sometimes, for convenience, I'll be using x_t:=x(t) The following is pretty emblematic of what I'm up to: def foo(t,y,x): if isinstance(x,float): return t*y*x else: return t*y*x(t) I'm going to be defining a lot of different functions foo that have the same behavior. Is there a clean way to do this in Python without rewriting the above code repeatedly? If I can also assert that x is either a float or a function, that would be great (maybe I should just raise an error or assert at the beginning of the definition?)
reference_answer: You can do this with a decorator. I've added parameters to the decorator to allow you to specify which argument should be t and which is x . import types def float_or_func(t_index=0, x_index=1): def decorator(func): def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): x = args[x_index] if isinstance(x, types.FunctionType): args = list(args) # convert from tuple to list so we can modify it args[x_index] = x(args[t_index]) elif isinstance(x, float): pass else: raise TypeError(f'{x} is not a float or function') return func(*args, **kwargs) return wrapper return decorator @float_or_func(t_index=0, x_index=2) def foo(t, y, x): return t*y*x print(foo(2, 3, 4.0)) # 24.0 print(foo(2, 3, lambda x: 5 * x)) # 60 print(foo(2, 3, 4)) # TypeError: 4 is not a float or function

question:
Please how do I compile a wxpython app that runs a flask server? The wxpython application does not work as it is supposed to work after compiling it with pyinstaller. When I run the python code with the python interpreter, it works properly. But when it is bundled into an app.exe, web.html2 does not render the flask web pages properly. Here is the code: # webview_app.py import wx import wx.html2 import threading from flask import Flask, render_template app = Flask(__name__) @app.route('/') def home(): return """ Bible Display Software

Bible Display Software

""" class MainFrame(wx.Frame): def __init__(self): super().__init__(parent=None, title='WxPython Flask App', size=(800, 600)) panel = wx.Panel(self) self.browser = wx.html2.WebView.New(panel) sizer = wx.BoxSizer(wx.VERTICAL) sizer.Add(self.browser, 1, wx.EXPAND) panel.SetSizer(sizer) self.browser.LoadURL("http://127.0.0.1:5000") def run_flask(): app.run(host='127.0.0.1', port=5000) def run_wx(): wx_app = wx.App() frame = MainFrame() frame.Show() wx_app.MainLoop() if __name__ == '__main__': flask_thread = threading.Thread(target=run_flask, daemon=True) flask_thread.start() run_wx() And belo
reference_answer: Pyinstaller would create a working EXE out of the box (brand-new, Python 3.13.1/PyInstaller 6.11.1), but it looked weird. Found out EXE uses wx.html2.WebViewBackendIE and not wx.html2.WebViewBackendEdge . Reason for this is PyInstaller does not copy the interfacing DLL \Lib\site-packages\wx\WebView2Loader.dll See this wxPython ticket for details What I did to get a EXE where Edge is used as backend rem change WINPYDIR to where your python is rem set WINPYDIR="C:\Program Files\python" pyinstaller ./app.py --distpath ./vdist -y --clean --contents-directory . --add-binary "%WINPYDIR%\Lib\site-packages\wx\WebView2Loader.dll:wx" Alternatively, the following was proposed on the wxPython Forum The absolute path can be avoided in the .spec file by: Add the following to the top of the .spec file from PyInstaller import HOMEPATH Use the relative path as follows: binaries=[(f’{HOMEPATH}/wx/WebView2Loader.dll’, ‘.’)],
llm_attempt: Two frozen-app-specific issues are most likely. First, a race condition: self.browser.LoadURL() fires immediately when the frame is created, but the bundled Flask server may not be listening yet (startup is slightly slower from a frozen exe), so WebView loads a connection-refused/blank page instead of your HTML - poll 127.0.0.1:5000 (or just delay ~0.5-1s) before calling LoadURL, or retry LoadURL on a timer until it succeeds. Second, if any part of your real app uses render_template with actual template/static files, PyInstaller won't bundle them automatically - add them explicitly via --add-data "templates;templates" --add-data "static;static" in the build command/spec. Also add app.run(..., use_reloader=False) - Flask's reloader spawns a subprocess that behaves badly under PyInstaller. Finally, wx.html2.WebView on Windows defaults to the legacy IE engine unless WebView2 is available/selected; if rendering (flex layout, modern CSS) looks wrong only in the exe, explicitly request the Edge backend with wx.html2.WebView.New(panel, backend=wx.html2.WebViewBackendEdge).

Passing Numeric Arrays to Python via ctypes Without Prior Knowledge of Array Length

I would like a C++ function return a numeric array ( uint8_t* converted from a vector) into a python bytes object. I don't know the length of this array ahead of time. This is numeric data, not a C string that would naturally have a null terminator. I'm having trouble finding any documentation on how to handle the length of the returned C pointer. Presumably, I can't just cast it to bytes since there's no length information in the bytes constructor. I'd like to avoid a really slow for loop. C++: uint8_t* cfunc(uint32_t* length_of_return_value); // returns an arbitrary-length numeric vector Python: import ctypes as c c.cdll.LoadLibrary("file.so") clib = c.CDLL("file.so") clib.cfunc.argtypes = [c.POINTER(c.c_uint32)] clib.cfunc.restype = c.POINTER(c.c_uint8) length_of_return_value = c.c_uint32(0) x = clib.cfunc(length_of_return_value) # now what? assert type(x) in {bytes, list}, "I need this to be a type that's convertible to numpy array"
reference_answer: There are a number of methods. Here are a few: Use ctypes.string_at with its size parameter when the returned value isn't null-terminated. It returns a bytes object as a copy of the original memory. Slice the returned pointer to the returned size. This returns a list of Python int representing the byte values in the array as a new Python object. Use numpy.ctypes.as_array and specify the shape parameter. This returns a numpy.ndarray object and shares the original data buffer instead of making a copy. Use this method if concerned about performance. Since you mentioned "I need this to be a type that's convertible to numpy array" I recommend the last method above and it will already be a numpy array. Make sure that if the returned value is an allocated array to free the memory when you are through with it. If using the first two methods above, you can free the memory immediately after making the copy, but if using the last shared memory method, do not free the memory until you are done with the numpy array. Working example (Windows): test.c: #include <stdint.h> #include <stdlib.h> __declspec(dllexport) uint8_t* cfunc(uint32_t* psize) { uint8_t* retval = malloc(5); for(uint8_t i = 0; i < 5; ++i) retval[i] = i; *psize = 5; return retval; } __declspec(dllexport) void cfree(uint8_t* p) { free(p); } test.py: import ctypes as ct import numpy as np clib = ct.CDLL('./test') clib.cfunc.argtypes = ct.POINTER(ct.c_uint32), clib.cfunc.restype = ct.POINTER(ct.c_uint8) clib.cfree.argtypes = ct.POINTER(ct.c_uint8), clib.cfree.restype = None size = ct.c_uint32(0) retval = clib.cfunc(size) # Us
llm_attempt:
Use ctypes.string_at(ptr, length) - it does a fast C-level memcpy into a Python bytes object, no Python loop needed:

length_of_return_value = c.c_uint32(0)
ptr = clib.cfunc(c.byref(length_of_return_value))
raw = c.string_at(ptr, length_of_return_value.value)  # bytes, exact length
arr = np.frombuffer(raw, dtype=np.uint8)

string_at works fine on non-string/binary data since you give it an explicit length - it doesn't stop at embedded null bytes. To avoid the extra copy, cast the pointer to a ctypes array of the right length and wrap with np.ctypeslib.as_array for a zero-copy view, then .copy() it before the C memory is freed: arr = np.ctypeslib.as_array(ptr, shape=(length_of_return_value.value,)).copy(). Important: the vector's underlying buffer was allocated on the C++ side, so Python won't free it - you need a matching C++ function (e.g. cfunc_free(ptr)) to release it after you've copied the data out, or you'll leak memory on every call.

reference_answer: Just trying to think about how my method 3b from this question works (since, obviously, it does the same as "3a" or any: compute function on a whole grid, and figure out where it is 0. But not just with a rough threshold, but with some fine interpolations), I read matplotlib doc. It it seems like matplotlib relies on contourpy to implement specific algorithm to do that. So you could use it too # Your function def function(x: float, y: float) -> float: return (x ** 2 + y ** 2 - 1) ** 3 - x ** 2 * y ** 3 X=np.linspace(-3,3,1000)[None,:] Y=np.linspace(-3,3,1000)[:,None] Z=function(X,Y) so now, Z is just a grid of 1000×1000 values of function(x,y) for x and y between -3 and 3. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt plt.imshow(Z) So the rough method would be to try to find a threshold ε, so that plotting any Z smaller than ε gives something that look like a line. If ε is too small, nothing will be plot, unless we are lucky enough to have function(x,y)=0 matching exactly some grid points. If ε is too large, we have a surface (well, whatever ε, it is a surface. But we want a surface thin enough to look like a line). plt.imshow(np.abs(Z)<0.01) Of course here we see the problem (more obviously than with the linked question: ε is both too small for some part of the shape and too high for some other. So, let's try what contourpy has to say import contourpy lines = contourpy.contour_generator(z=Z).lines(0) for l in lines: plt.plot(l[:,0], l[:,1]) Here it is :D Note that imshow shows y axis downward, while plot use, by default, y axis upward, as tradition with image and charts. Hence the upsid

A practical approach: evaluate f on a regular voxel grid with numpy (vectorized, not nested loops), and mark a voxel filled where f is within an adaptive threshold of zero, using the local gradient magnitude so the shell stays about one voxel thick regardless of how steeply f is scaled:

def rasterize_implicit(f, xr, yr, zr, res=1):
    xs, ys, zs = (np.arange(*r, res) for r in (xr, yr, zr))
    X, Y, Z = np.meshgrid(xs, ys, zs, indexing='ij')
    F = f(X, Y, Z)
    gx, gy, gz = np.gradient(F, res)
    grad = np.sqrt(gx**2+gy**2+gz**2) + 1e-9
    mask = np.abs(F) < grad * res * 0.5
    return {tuple(p) for p in np.argwhere(mask)}

This handles any implicit f(x,y,z)=0 without special-casing each shape; ordinary z=f(x,y) and parametric forms work once converted to implicit form. For a filled solid instead of a shell, keep voxels where f<0. If you need a watertight mesh first, skimage.measure.marching_cubes on the same grid is the standard alternative, then voxelize its triangles.

question:
Best practices for structuring Django REST APIs for maintainability and scalability

I am building a Django-based backend for an e-commerce project with multiple models and REST API endpoints. I want to follow clean architecture and maintainability best practices. How should I structure views, serializers, and URLs for scalability and easier debugging? Tags: Python, Django, REST-API, Backend
reference_answer: It is always better to separate the applications (users/payment/categories etc) and keep its core logic inside itself. I think for a big project it is not good to put all the models, serializers or urls into a single module named api.
llm_attempt: For a maintainable DRF backend: one Django app per bounded context (orders, products, users, payments), not one giant app. Within each app keep models.py, serializers.py, and either views.py (APIView/generics) or viewsets.py + routers if the API is CRUD-heavy - routers auto-generate consistent URLs and cut boilerplate. Keep views/viewsets thin: put business logic in a services.py (writes/side effects) and selectors.py (reads/complex queries) layer instead of fat views or fat models, which makes logic testable independent of HTTP. Use nested serializers or separate read/write serializers when input and output shapes differ. Version the API (api/v1/...), centralize permission/authentication classes and a custom exception handler, add pagination and filtering (django-filter) by default, and generate docs with drf-spectacular. Split settings into base/dev/prod, move slow work to Celery, and write tests per app (models, serializers, views separately). This mirrors Two Scoops of Django / DRF community conventions and scales well as the number of endpoints grows.

question:
How to avoid IntegrityError issue with update_or_create?

I would appreciate it if someone could explain why I'm having IntegrityError exception being thrown here, and how to avoid it. When an object already exists, isn't the update_or_create method supposed to update it ? models.py class OHLCV(TimestampedModel): market = models.ForeignKey(Market, on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name='candles', null=True) index = models.ForeignKey(Index, on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name='candles', null=True) timeframe = models.CharField(max_length=10) open, high, low, close, volume = [models.FloatField(null=True) for i in range(5)] datetime = models.DateTimeField(null=True) class Meta: verbose_name_plural = "OHLCV" unique_together = [['market', 'timeframe', 'datetime'], ['index', 'timeframe', 'datetime']] tasks.py @app.task def bulk_update_ohlcv(timeframe): for obj in Market.objects.filter(active=True): if obj.exchange.is_status_ok(): update_ohlcv.delay('market', obj.pk, timeframe) @app.task def update_ohlcv(self, type, pk, timeframe): [code here] if obj.__class__ == Market: ohlcv, created = OHLCV.objects.update_or_create(market=obj, timeframe=timeframe, datetime=dt, open=candle[1], defaults=defaults ) elif obj.__class__ == Index: ohlcv, created = OHLCV.objects.update_or_create(index=obj, timeframe=timeframe, datetime=dt, open=candle[1], defaults=defaults ) Error: -celery_worker-1 | 2023-04-01T06:55:47.710298043Z IntegrityError: duplicate key value violates unique constraint -celery_worker-1 | 2023-04-01T06:55:47.710302260Z "market_ohlcv_market_id_timeframe_datetime_8ffd84de_uniq" -celery_worker-1 | 2023-04-01T06:55:47.710306227Z DETAIL: K
reference_answer: The issue lies with the open field being in the kwargs of the update_or_create . Django will try to get an OHLCV matching the four fields market , timeframe , datetime and open . If there is a instance matching the first three and not open , Django will create a new instance clashing with your constraint. You'll need to either move the open field to the default dictionnary or include it in the unique together constraint

reference_answer: You mostly write lambdas inline as arguments to functions, without assigning them to a name as in your example. That's the main point of that syntax compared to function def initions. Code like this is common and useful: bars = filter(lambda i: i.foo == 'bar', some_list)
llm_attempt: Self-contained equality lambdas (no outer variable) are common wherever a boolean predicate is needed as a value, most often as the key/predicate argument to another function: filter(lambda x: x == 0, values), sorted(data, key=lambda d: d['status'] == 'done') (pushes matching items to one end), any(map(lambda x: x is None, row)), or all(...)-style checks written as lambdas passed into custom validators. question:
FastAPI route works locally with `/` but not on Vercel (and vice versa)

I have a FastAPI + Next.js project deployed on Vercel. Locally everything works, but on Vercel some routes break depending on whether I use a trailing slash in the route definition. For example, in my usrs.py router: from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends from ..schemas.user import UserOut from ..auth import require_admin from ..repositories.users import list_users user_router = APIRouter(prefix="/users", tags=["users"]) @user_router.get("/", response_model=list[UserOut]) def get_users(_: UserOut = Depends(require_admin)): return list_users() Locally (Uvicorn) GET http://localhost:8001/api/users/ works. GET http://localhost:8001/api/users redirects to /users/ as expected. On Vercel (serverless FastAPI): GET https://myapp.vercel.app/api/users/ → 500 GET https://myapp.vercel.app/api/users 404 or .vercel.app/api/users/ net::ERR_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS So I tried removing the slash in the route definition: @user_router.get("", response_model=list[UserOut]) def get_users(_: UserOut = Depends(require_admin)): return list_users() Now it works on Vercel, but fails locally (404). What I’ve checked DB and schema are fine ( /api/db-check and /api/_schema_status return OK). Other endpoints like /api/healthz and /api/users/login work fine. My next.config.js proxies /api/:path* → FastAPI in dev, and Vercel vercel.json routes /api/(.*) → /api/index.py . Question Why is there this incompatibility between local and Vercel regarding trailing slashes? How can I define my FastAPI routes so they work both locally and on Vercel without having to change code?
reference_answer: I resolved this issue. I've run into the "tailing-slash" mismatch between FastAPI/Starlette and the way Vercel normalize paths. Locally: FastAPI' default RedirectSlashes middleware happily 307-redirects /api/users -> /api/users/ . My route with @get("/") then matches and works. On vercel: something in the edge/proxy stack (rewrite, CDN, or your client) is hitting /api/users without the slash and the redirect either (a) gets stripped/looped or (b) never happens the same way. So only a route declared at "" matches reliably there. The robust fix (works everywhere) Turn off auto redirecting and Serve both paths for every collection endpoint \# main/index.py from fastapi import FastAPI app = FastAPI(title=settings.APP_TITLE, lifespan=lifespan, redirect_slashes=False) # routes/users.py from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends from ..schemas.user import UserOut from ..auth import require_admin user_router = APIRouter(prefix="/users", tags=["users"]) @user_router.get("", include_in_schema=False, response_model=list[UserOut]) # /api/users @user_router.get("/", response_model=list[UserOut]) # /api/users/ def get_users(_: UserOut = Depends(require_admin)): return list_users() This dual-decorator pattern for the users collection resolved above issue. This removes the ambiguity and avoids relying on redirects that may be handled differently by Vercel.
llm_attempt: This is FastAPI/Starlette's automatic trailing-slash redirect (redirect_slashes=True by default) interacting badly with Vercel's serverless routing. Locally, Uvicorn happily issues a 307 redirect between /users and /users/ and your client follows it. On Vercel, your vercel.json already rewrites /api/(.*) to a single serverless function, so when FastAPI then tries to 307-redirect internally, it can conflict with or get re-wrapped by that rewrite, producing the 500/404/redirect-loop you're seeing - serverless platforms often don't preserve this redirect behavior the way a persistent dev server does. The reliable fix is to stop relying on the redirect at all: set app = FastAPI(redirect_slashes=False), then register the route without a trailing slash, @user_router.get(""), and make sure both your Next.js proxy config and any client fetch calls request that exact path (no trailing slash) consistently. That way the same route definition behaves identically locally and on Vercel, since no redirect is ever triggered in either environment.

question:
Why does Django give a warning about unapplied migrations and how to fix it?

I started learning Django and i find a warning message: " You have 18 unapplied migration(s). Your project may not work properly until you apply the migrations for app(s): admin, auth, contenttypes, sessions. Run 'python manage.py migrate' to apply them.". What is the reason behind this warnings Just want to know this
reference_answer: Every time you modify a model, you should execute ./manage.py makemigrations and ./manage.py migrate . Make migrations creates one or more migrations in <app>/migrations , where <app> is the app which defined the changed model. If you import a package or an app from some other Django project, its migrations won't have been applied on your database. Ditto, if you move from accessing one database to another. ./manage.py showmigrations will show you your migrations, IIRC including unapplied ones. ./manage.py migrate ought to fix the warning by making the database compatible with the migrations. For more information, consult the documentation .
llm_attempt:
This warning means your database's schema doesn't yet match Django's models for those apps. Migration files (under each app's migrations/ folder) describe how to create/alter database tables; Django ships built-in apps (admin, auth, contenttypes, sessions) with their own migrations that create tables like auth_user, django_session, etc. Until you actually run them, those tables don't exist in your database, so features depending on them (login, the admin site, sessions, permissions) will error with something like 'no such table.' Fix it by running:

python manage.py migrate

This applies all pending migrations, including your own apps' if you have any. If you've changed your own models and don't yet have migration files for those changes, run python manage.py makemigrations first, then migrate. This is a routine, expected step after starting a new Django project or pulling in model changes - not something broken.

Before actually executing the function for every element of the input array, ie np.array([np.uint8(1)]) , it takes the first element of it (ie np.uint8(1) ), runs the function to check the output type and size. More info in this thread or in the docs . After having run the function for the first element, it iterates over all elements. So, it takes the first element again. My surprise is that now the first element is an int , not a numpy.uint8 value, as per the third line of the above print. (This one: x is 1 and has type <class 'int'> ). Of course, no dtype exists on an int, because its not a numpy dtype, but a Python scalar (that's why the 4th line is no dtype exists on x ). This behaviour does not happen when the input np.uint8(1) is not the element of a np.array([]) , but is a list or not even an iterable. These two lines below: res = np.vectorize(f)([np.uint8(1)]) # res: array([1], dtype=uint8) res = np.vectorize(f)(np.uint8(1)) # res: array(1, dtype=uint8) both result in these pr
llm_attempt: This is an internals quirk of np.vectorize, not documented behavior to rely on. Without explicit otypes, vectorize first makes a 'trial call' on one element to infer the output dtype - that lookup uses plain array indexing (arr[0]), which preserves the numpy scalar subtype (numpy.uint8). The real elementwise pass then runs through numpy.frompyfunc, which builds a generic object-dtype ufunc and iterates via the broadcasting machinery; unboxing elements from a fixed-dtype array into that object-dtype pipeline yields native Python int instead of the numpy scalar wrapper. With list or scalar input there's no dtype-typed source array to unbox from the same way, so the original np.uint8 instance passes through unchanged both times. This is implementation detail of a function whose own docs say it exists 'primarily for convenience, not for performance', and it can differ across numpy versions. If consistent scalar types matter, avoid np.vectorize - use np.frompyfunc directly with an explicit cast, or write the loop with np.nditer specifying op_dtypes.
